object.defect: None. The scenario is a standard sampling-distribution setup: each dot is the mean of a sample of size n, so the dotplot displays the sampling distribution of x̄. By the Central Limit Theorem, that distribution approaches normality as n grows (mean μ, standard deviation σ/√n) regardless of the population's right skew, while the population distribution itself is unchanged. false_statements.quote: The dotplot shows the population distribution of delivery times; the Central Limit Theorem makes that population approximately normal as n grows.
false_statements.why: The dotplot displays the mean of each possible sample, so it shows the sampling distribution of the sample mean, not the population distribution of individual delivery times. The Central Limit Theorem describes the shape of the sampling distribution of the sample mean as sample size increases; it does not alter the population distribution, which remains right-skewed regardless of n.

false_statements.quote: The dotplot shows the distribution of individual delivery times in one sample; the Central Limit Theorem makes those observations approximately normal as n grows.
false_statements.why: The dotplot aggregates means from all possible samples of size n, not raw observations from a single sample. The Central Limit Theorem does not imply that individual observations within a sample become normally distributed; it concerns the distribution of sample means across many samples.

false_statements.quote: it must remain strongly right-skewed as n grows because the population is right-skewed
false_statements.why: While the population is right-skewed, the Central Limit Theorem states that the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes more approximately normal as the sample size increases, not that it retains the population's skewness.
